h: Jewels, swords and a lady with ivory bangles
p: The Yorkshire Museum has been around a while. It opened in 1830, built by the Yorkshire Philosophical Society, a group of local gentlemen fascinated by science and history, and it was one of the earliest purpose-built museums in the country. The grand columned front facing the gardens is a big part of its charm.

There are a few objects worth seeking out. The Middleham Jewel is a fifteenth-century gold pendant set with a large sapphire, found by a metal detectorist near Middleham Castle, the home of Richard III. The Cawood Sword is a beautifully preserved Viking-age blade pulled from the River Ouse, and the Anglo-Saxon Coppergate Helmet, found during building work in York, is one of the finest of its kind. The Vale of York Hoard, a stash of Viking silver and coins buried in a decorated cup, is also often on show here.

Roman fans should look out for the story of the Ivory Bangle Lady, a wealthy woman buried in Roman York whose remains suggest she had North African roots, a striking reminder of how diverse the city was nearly two thousand years ago. York has another big Roman connection: Constantine the Great was proclaimed emperor here in 306, and there's a statue of him outside the Minster.
For the Jurassic galleries, keep an eye out for the marine reptiles found along the Yorkshire coast around Whitby.
Allow an hour and a half to two hours. Afterwards, look out for the Multangular Tower in the Museum Gardens, part of the Roman fortress walls, then head across Exhibition Square to York Art Gallery.
